danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 12
paragraphs: Efter henrettelsen blev Pierre adskilt fra de øvrige fanger og anbragt alene i en lille, ødelagt og tilsølet kirke.

Hen mod aften kom en underofficer ind med to soldater og meddelte ham, at han var benådet og nu ville komme i krigsfangebarakken. Uden at forstå, hvad der blev sagt til ham, rejste Pierre sig og gik med soldaterne. De førte ham til den øvre ende af marken, hvor der var opført nogle skure af forkullede planker, bjælker og lægter, og førte ham ind i et af dem. I mørket omringede en tyve forskellige mænd Pierre. Han så på dem uden at forstå, hvem de var, hvorfor de var der, eller hvad de ville ham. Han hørte, hvad de sagde, men forstod ikke meningen med ordene og drog ingen slutninger eller anvendelser af dem. Han svarede på spørgsmål, de stillede ham, men overvejede ikke, hvem der lyttede til hans svar, eller hvordan de ville opfatte dem. Han betragtede deres ansigter og skikkelser, men de forekom ham alle lige meningsløse.

Fra det øjeblik Pierre havde været vidne til de forfærdelige mord begået af mænd, der ikke ønskede at begå dem, var det, som om hovedfjederen i hans liv, som alt afhang af, og som fik alt til at synes levende, pludselig var revet ud, og alt var styrtet sammen i en bunke af meningsløst affald. Skønt han ikke erkendte det over for sig selv, var hans tro på universets rette orden, på menneskeheden, på sin egen sjæl og på Gud blevet ødelagt. Han havde oplevet dette før, men aldrig så stærkt som nu. Når lignende tvivl tidligere havde angrebet ham, havde de været resultat af hans egne fejltagelser, og i sit hjertes dyb havde han følt, at lindring for hans fortvivlelse og for disse tvivl var at finde i ham selv. Men nu følte han, at universet var styrtet sammen for hans øjne, og kun meningsløse ruiner var tilbage, og dette var ikke hans skyld. Han følte, at det ikke stod i hans magt at genvinde troen på livets mening.

Rundt om ham i mørket stod mænd, og noget ved ham interesserede dem tydeligvis meget. De fortalte ham noget og spurgte ham om noget. Så førte de ham et sted hen, og til sidst befandt han sig i et hjørne af skuret blandt mænd, der lo og talte på alle sider.
»Nå, så var det ham, kammerater... den fyrste, som...« sagde en stemme i den anden ende af skuret med stærkt eftertryk på ordet som.

Pierre sad stille og ubevægeligt på en bunke halm op ad væggen og åbnede og lukkede øjnene af og til. Men så snart han lukkede dem, så han foran sig fabriksknægtens forfærdelige ansigt — forfærdeligt især på grund af dets enfoldighed — og ansigterne på morderne, endnu mere forfærdelige på grund af deres uro. Og han åbnede øjnene igen og stirrede tomt ud i mørket omkring sig.

Ved siden af ham i sammenkrøbet stilling sad en lille mand, hvis tilstedeværelse han først blev opmærksom på ved en stærk lugt af sved, der kom fra ham, hver gang han rørte sig. Denne mand foretog sig noget med sine ben i mørket, og skønt Pierre ikke kunne se hans ansigt, fornam han, at manden uophørligt skottede til ham. Da Pierre var blevet vant til mørket, så han, at manden viklede sine benviklinger af, og den måde, han gjorde det på, vakte Pierres interesse.

Da han havde viklet snoren af, der bandt viklingen på det ene ben, oprullede han den omhyggeligt og satte straks i gang med det andet ben, idet han skottede op til Pierre. Mens den ene hånd hang den første snor op, var den anden allerede i gang med at vikle viklingen af det andet ben. På denne måde, efter omhyggeligt at have fjernet benviklingerne med behændige cirkulære bevægelser af armen, der fulgte hinanden uafbrudt, hængte manden viklingerne op på nogle pløkker over sit hoved. Derefter tog han en kniv frem, skar noget af, lukkede kniven, lagde den under sit hovedgærde, og satte sig bekvemt til rette med armene om de løftede knæ og blikket fæstnet på Pierre. Denne fornam noget behageligt, trøstende og afrundet i disse behændige bevægelser, i mandens velordnede indretning af sit hjørne, og selv i hans lugt, og han betragtede manden uden at tage øjnene fra ham.
»De har set mange trængsler, hr., ikke sandt?« sagde den lille mand pludselig.

Og der var så megen venlighed og enfoldighed i hans syngende stemme, at Pierre ville svare, men hans kæbe skælvede, og han følte tårerne stige. Den lille mand, der ikke gav Pierre tid til at røbe sin forvirring, fortsatte øjeblikkeligt i den samme behagelige tone:

»Nå, nå, lille ven, vær ikke ked af det!« sagde han med den ømme, syngende, kælne stemme, som gamle russiske bondekoner bruger. »Vær ikke ked af det, ven — 'lid en time, lev i en evighed!' sådan er det, min kære. Og her lever vi, Gudskelov, uden fortræd. Blandt disse folk er der også gode mennesker såvel som dårlige,« sagde han, og mens han stadig talte, drejede han sig på knæene med en smidig bevægelse, rejste sig, hostede og gik hen til en anden del af skuret.
»Nå, din slyngel!« hørte Pierre den samme venlige stemme sige i den anden ende af skuret. »Så er du kommet, din slyngel? Hun husker... Nå, nå, det er nok!«
Og soldaten, der skubbede en lille hund fra sig, som hoppede op ad ham, vendte tilbage til sin plads og satte sig. I hænderne havde han noget pakket ind i en klud.
»Værsgo, spis lidt, hr.,« sagde han og genoptog sin tidligere respektfulde tone, idet han pakkede op og rakte Pierre nogle bagte kartofler. »Vi havde suppe til middag, og kartoflerne er glimrende!«
Pierre havde ikke spist hele dagen, og lugten af kartoflerne forekom ham overordentlig behagelig. Han takkede soldaten og begyndte at spise.
»Nå, smager de?« sagde soldaten med et smil. »De skal gøre det sådan her.«
Han tog en kartoffel, trak sin lommekniv frem, skar kartoflen i to lige halvdele på sin håndflade, dryssede lidt salt på fra kluden og rakte den til Pierre.
»Kartoflerne er glimrende!« sagde han endnu engang. »Spis dem sådan!«
Pierre syntes, han aldrig havde spist noget, der smagte bedre.
»Åh, mig fejler intet,« sagde han, »men hvorfor skød de de stakkels mennesker? Den sidste var knap tyve.«

»Ts, ts...!« sagde den lille mand. »Ah, hvilken synd... hvilken synd!« tilføjede han hurtigt, og som om hans ord altid lå parate i hans mund og fløj ud af sig selv, fortsatte han: »Hvordan gik det til, hr., at De blev i Moskva?«
»Jeg troede ikke, de ville komme så hurtigt. Jeg blev tilfældigt,« svarede Pierre.
»Og hvordan arresterede de Dem, kære ven? I Deres hjem?«
»Nej, jeg gik ud for at se branden, og de arresterede mig dér og stillede mig for retten som brandstifter.«
»Hvor der er lov, er der uret,« skød den lille mand ind.
»Og har De været her længe?« spurgte Pierre, mens han tyggende spiste den sidste kartoffel.
»Jeg? Det var i søndags, de tog mig, fra et lazaret i Moskva.«
»Nå, er De soldat?«
»Ja, vi er soldater af Ápsjeron-regimentet. Jeg lå for døden af feber. Vi fik intet at vide. Der lå en tyve stykker af os. Vi anede intet, havde slet ikke forestillet os det.«
»Og er De trist her?« spurgte Pierre.

»Hvordan kan man lade være, lille ven? Mit navn er Platón, og efternavnet er Karatajev,« tilføjede han, tydeligvis for at gøre det lettere for Pierre at tiltale ham. »De kalder mig 'lille falk' i regimentet. Hvordan kan man lade være med at være trist? Moskva — hun er byernes moder. Hvordan kan man se alt det her og ikke være trist? Men 'maddiken gnaver kålen, men dør først selv'; det sagde de gamle altid,« tilføjede han hurtigt.
»Hvad? Hvad sagde De?« spurgte Pierre.
»Hvem? Jeg?« sagde Karatajev. »Jeg siger, at tingene sker, ikke som vi planlægger, men som Gud bestemmer,« svarede han i den tro, at han gentog, hvad han havde sagt før, og fortsatte straks:
»Nå, og De, har De en ejendom, hr.? Og et hus? Så De har overflod? Og en husmoder? Og Deres gamle forældre, lever de endnu?« spurgte han.

Og skønt det var for mørkt til, at Pierre kunne se, fornam han, at et undertrykt smil af venlighed spillede om soldatens læber, mens han stillede disse spørgsmål. Han virkede bedrøvet over, at Pierre ikke havde forældre, især ikke en moder.
»En kone til råd, en svigermoder til velkomst, men ingen er så kær som ens egen moder!« sagde han. »Nå, og har De småfolk?« fortsatte han.
Igen syntes Pierres benægtende svar at bedrøve ham, og han skyndte sig at tilføje:
»Tager De det ikke tungt! De er unge folk endnu, og Gud give, De endnu må få nogle. Det vigtigste er at leve i harmoni....«
»Men det er jo alt sammen lige meget nu,« kunne Pierre ikke lade være med at sige.
»Åh, min kære ven!« sagde Karatajev. »Sig aldrig nej til et fængsel eller en tiggersæk!«
Han satte sig mere bekvemt til rette og hostede, tydeligvis i færd med at forberede sig på at fortælle en lang historie.

»Jamen, min kære ven, jeg boede stadig hjemme,« begyndte han. »Vi havde en velsitueret gård, masser af jord, vi bønder levede godt, og vores hus var et hus, man kunne takke Gud for. Når Far og vi gik ud at slå hø, var vi syv. Vi levede godt. Vi var rigtige bønder. Og så skete det...«

Og Platón Karatajev fortalte en lang historie om, hvordan han var gået ind i en andens lund for at hugge brænde, hvordan han var blevet snappet af skovfogeden, var stillet for retten, pisket og sendt i militærtjeneste.

»Jamen, lille ven,« og et smil ændrede tonen i hans stemme, »vi troede, det var en ulykke, men det viste sig at være en velsignelse! Havde det ikke været for min synd, ville min bror have måttet gå som soldat. Men han, min lillebror, havde fem smårollinger, mens jeg, ser du, kun efterlod en kone. Vi havde en lille pige, men Gud tog hende, inden jeg kom af sted som soldat. Jeg kommer hjem på orlov, og jeg skal fortælle dig, hvordan det var, jeg kigger og ser, at de lever bedre end før. Gården fuld af kvæg, kvinderne derhjemme, to brødre ude og tjene penge, og kun Mikhail, den yngste, hjemme. Far, siger han, 'Alle mine børn er mig lige kære: det gør lige ondt, ligegyldig hvilken finger der bides i. Men hvis Platón ikke var blevet barberet til soldat, ville Mikhail have måttet gå.' Han kaldte os alle sammen og, vil du tro det, stillede os op foran ikonerne. 'Mikhail,' siger han, 'kom herhen og bøj dig for hans fødder; og du, unge kone, bøj dig også; og I, børnebørn, bøj jer også for ham! Forstår I?' siger han. Sådan er det, kære ven. Skæbnen søger et hoved. Men vi sidder altid og dømmer: 'det er ikke godt — det er ikke rigtigt!' Vores lykke er som vand i et net: man trækker i det, og det buler ud, men når man har trukket det op, er det tomt! Sådan er det.«
Og Platón rykkede sig på halmen.
Efter en kort stilhed rejste han sig.
»Nå, jeg tænker, De er søvnig,« sagde han og begyndte hurtigt at korse sig og gentage:

»Herre Jesus Kristus, hellige Nikolaj, Frola og Lavra! Herre Jesus Kristus, hellige Nikolaj, Frola og Lavra! Herre Jesus Kristus, forbarm Dig over os og frels os!« sluttede han, bøjede sig til jorden, rejste sig, sukkede og satte sig atter på sin bunke halm. »Sådan. Læg mig ned som en sten, oh Gud, og rejs mig op som et brød,« mumlede han, mens han lagde sig ned og trak frakken over sig.
»Hvilken bøn var det, De bad?« spurgte Pierre.
»Hvad?« mumlede Platón, der allerede var ved at falde i søvn. »Hvad sagde jeg? Jeg bad. Beder De ikke?«
»Jo, det gør jeg,« sagde Pierre. »Men hvad var det, De sagde: Frola og Lavra?«

»Nå, selvfølgelig,« svarede Platón hurtigt, »hestenes helgener. Man skal også have medlidenhed med dyrene. Nå, din slyngel! Nu har du lagt dig til rette og fået varmen, din tæveunge!« sagde Karatajev, idet han rørte ved hunden, der lå ved hans fødder, og vendte sig atter om og faldt straks i søvn.

Gråd og skrig hørtes et sted langt borte udenfor, og flammer var synlige gennem sprækker i skuret, men indenfor var der stille og mørkt. Længe lå Pierre vågen med åbne øjne i mørket og lyttede til Platóns regelmæssige snorken ved sin side, og han følte, at den verden, der var styrtet sammen, atter rørte sig i hans sjæl med en ny skønhed og på nye og urokkelige grundvolde.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: After the execution, Pierre was separated from the rest of the prisoners and placed alone in a small, ruined, and filthy church.

Toward evening a noncommissioned officer entered with two soldiers and told him that he had been pardoned and would now go to the barracks for prisoners of war. Without understanding what was said to him, Pierre got up and went with the soldiers. They took him to the upper end of the field, where there were some sheds built of charred planks, beams, and scraps of wood, and led him into one of them. In the darkness some twenty different men surrounded Pierre. He looked at them without understanding who they were, why they were there, or what they wanted. He heard what they said but did not grasp the meaning of the words and drew no kind of conclusions from them. He replied to questions they put to him but did not consider who was listening or how they would understand his replies. He looked at their faces and figures, but they all seemed equally meaningless to him.

From the moment Pierre had witnessed those terrible murders committed by men who did not wish to commit them, it was as if the mainspring of his life, on which everything depended and which made everything appear alive, had suddenly been wrenched out and everything had collapsed into a heap of meaningless debris. Though he did not acknowledge it to himself, his faith in the right ordering of the universe, in humanity, in his own soul, and in God had been destroyed. He had experienced this before, but never so powerfully. Previously, when similar doubts had assailed him, they had been the result of his own wrongdoing, and at the bottom of his heart he had felt that relief from despair and doubt was to be found within himself. But now he felt that the universe had crumbled before his eyes and only meaningless ruins remained—and this through no fault of his own. He felt that it was not in his power to regain faith in the meaning of life.

Around him in the darkness men were standing, and evidently something about him interested them greatly. They were telling him something and asking him something. Then they led him away somewhere, and at last he found himself in a corner of the shed among men who were laughing and talking on all sides.
"Well, then, mates... that very prince who..." some voice at the other end of the shed was saying, with a strong emphasis on the word who.

Sitting silent and motionless on a heap of straw against the wall, Pierre sometimes opened and sometimes closed his eyes. But as soon as he closed them he saw before him the dreadful face of the factory boy—especially dreadful because of its simplicity—and the faces of the murderers, even more dreadful because of their unease. And he opened his eyes again and stared blankly into the darkness around him.

Beside him, in a stooping position, sat a small man whose presence Pierre first became aware of through a strong smell of sweat that came from him every time he moved. This man was doing something to his legs in the darkness, and though Pierre could not see his face, he sensed that the man kept glancing at him. Growing accustomed to the darkness, Pierre saw that the man was taking off his leg wrappings, and the way he did it aroused Pierre's interest.

Having unwound the string that tied the wrapping on one leg, he carefully coiled it up and immediately set to work on the other leg, glancing up at Pierre. While one hand hung up the first string, the other was already unwinding the wrapping on the second leg. In this way, having carefully removed the leg wrappings with deft circular motions of his arm following one another without interruption, the man hung them up on some pegs fixed above his head. Then he took out a knife, cut something, closed the knife, placed it under the head of his bed, and seating himself comfortably, clasped his arms around his raised knees and fixed his eyes on Pierre. Pierre was conscious of something pleasant, comforting, and well-rounded in these deft movements, in the man's well-ordered arrangements in his corner, and even in his very smell, and he looked at the man without taking his eyes off him.
"You've seen a lot of trouble, sir, haven't you?" the little man suddenly said.

And there was so much kindness and simplicity in his singsong voice that Pierre tried to reply, but his jaw trembled and he felt tears rising to his eyes. The little fellow, giving Pierre no time to show his emotion, instantly continued in the same pleasant tones:

"Eh, lad, don't fret!" said he, in the tender, singsong, caressing voice old Russian peasant women use. "Don't fret, friend—'suffer an hour, live for a lifetime!' That's how it is, my dear fellow. And here we live, thank God, without offense. Among these folk too there are good men as well as bad," said he, and still speaking, he turned on his knees with a supple movement, got up, coughed, and went off to another part of the shed.
"Hey, you rascal!" Pierre heard the same kind voice saying at the other end of the shed. "So you've come back, you rascal? She remembers... Now, now, that'll do!"
And the soldier, pushing away a little dog that was jumping up at him, returned to his place and sat down. In his hands he had something wrapped in a rag.
"Here, have a bite, sir," said he, resuming his former respectful tone as he unwrapped and offered Pierre some baked potatoes. "We had soup for dinner and the potatoes are wonderful!"
Pierre had not eaten all day, and the smell of the potatoes seemed extremely pleasant. He thanked the soldier and began to eat.
"Well, are they all right?" said the soldier with a smile. "You should try it this way."
He took a potato, drew out his clasp knife, cut it into two equal halves on the palm of his hand, sprinkled some salt on it from the rag, and handed it to Pierre.
"The potatoes are wonderful!" he said once more. "Try some like that!"
Pierre thought he had never eaten anything that tasted better.
"Oh, I'm all right," said he, "but why did they shoot those poor men? The last one was barely twenty."

"Tsk, tsk..." said the little man. "Ah, what a sin... what a sin!" he added quickly, and as if his words were always waiting ready in his mouth and flew out of their own accord, he went on: "How is it, sir, that you stayed in Moscow?"
"I didn't think they would come so soon. I stayed by accident," replied Pierre.
"And how did they arrest you, dear fellow? At your house?"
"No, I went to look at the fire, and they arrested me there and tried me as an arsonist."
"Where there's law, there's injustice," put in the little man.
"And have you been here long?" Pierre asked, munching the last of the potato.
"Me? It was last Sunday they took me, out of a hospital in Moscow."
"Why, are you a soldier then?"
"Yes, we are soldiers of the Apsheron regiment. I was dying of fever. We weren't told anything. There were some twenty of us lying there. We had no idea, never guessed at all."
"And do you feel sad here?" Pierre asked.

"How can one not feel sad, lad? My name is Platon, and the surname is Karataev," he added, evidently wanting to make it easier for Pierre to address him. "They call me 'little falcon' in the regiment. How can one not feel sad? Moscow—she's the mother of cities. How can one see all this and not feel sad? But 'the worm gnaws the cabbage, yet dies first'; that's what the old folks used to tell us," he added quickly.
"What? What did you say?" asked Pierre.
"Who? Me?" said Karataev. "I say things happen not as we plan but as God decides," he replied, thinking he was repeating what he had said before, and immediately continued:
"Well, and you, sir, do you have an estate? And a house? So you're well-off, then? And a wife? And are your old parents still living?" he asked.

And though it was too dark for Pierre to see, he felt that a suppressed smile of kindliness puckered the soldier's lips as he asked these questions. He seemed saddened that Pierre had no parents, especially no mother.
"A wife for counsel, a mother-in-law for welcome, but there's none so dear as one's own mother!" said he. "Well, and do you have little ones?" he went on asking.
Again Pierre's negative answer seemed to distress him, and he hastened to add:
"Never mind! You're young folks yet, and God willing you may still have some. The main thing is to live in harmony..."
"But it's all the same now," Pierre could not help saying.
"Ah, my dear fellow!" replied Karataev. "Never refuse a prison cell or a beggar's sack!"
He settled himself more comfortably and coughed, evidently preparing to tell a long story.

"Well, my dear fellow, I was still living at home," he began. "We had a prosperous homestead, plenty of land; we peasants lived well and our house was one to thank God for. When Father and we went out mowing, there were seven of us. We lived well. We were real peasants. It so happened..."
And Platon Karataev told a long story of how he had gone into someone's woods to take firewood, how he had been caught by the gamekeeper, was tried, flogged, and sent to serve as a soldier.

"Well, lad," and a smile changed the tone of his voice, "we thought it was a misfortune but it turned out a blessing! If it hadn't been for my sin, my brother would have had to go as a soldier. But he, my younger brother, had five little ones, while I, you see, only left a wife behind. We had a little girl, but God took her before I went as a soldier. I came home on leave and I'll tell you how it was—I look and see that they're living better than before. The yard full of livestock, the women at home, two brothers away earning wages, and only Mikhail, the youngest, at home. Father said, 'All my children are the same to me: it hurts the same whichever finger gets bitten. But if Platon hadn't been shaved for a soldier, Mikhail would have had to go.' He called us all before the icons. 'Mikhail,' he says, 'come here and bow at his feet; and you, young woman, bow down too; and you, grandchildren, also bow before him! Do you understand?' he says. That's how it is, dear fellow. Fate looks for a head. But we are always judging, 'that's not right, this isn't fair!' Our luck is like water in a net: you pull and it bulges, but when you've drawn it out, it's empty! That's how it is."
And Platon shifted his seat on the straw.
After a short silence he rose.
"Well, I think you must be sleepy," said he, and began rapidly crossing himself, repeating:

"Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, holy Saint Nicholas, Frola and Lavra! Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on us and save us!" he concluded, then bowed to the ground, got up, sighed, and sat down again on his heap of straw. "That's the way. Lay me down like a stone, O God, and raise me up like a loaf," he muttered as he lay down, pulling his coat over himself.
"What prayer was that you were saying?" asked Pierre.
"Eh?" murmured Platon, who had almost fallen asleep. "What was I saying? I was praying. Don't you pray?"
"Yes, I do," said Pierre. "But what was that you said: Frola and Lavra?"

"Well, of course," replied Platon quickly, "the horses' saints. One must have pity on the animals too. Hey, you rascal! Now you've curled up and got warm, you daughter of a..." said Karataev, touching the dog that lay at his feet, and again turning over, he fell asleep immediately.

Sounds of crying and screaming came from somewhere in the distance outside, and flames were visible through the cracks of the shed, but inside it was quiet and dark. For a long time Pierre did not sleep but lay with eyes open in the darkness, listening to the steady snoring of Platon beside him, and he felt that the world that had been shattered was once more stirring in his soul with a new beauty and on new and unshakable foundations.
